newsitem.title: USA: Dole calls for affirmative action changes in Calif.
newsitem.headline: Dole calls for affirmative action changes in Calif.

text.p: Saying racial quotas "pit one American against another," Bob Dole on Monday issued a strong call to end some affirmative action programmes favoured by U.S. President Bill Clinton.

Lagging in the polls with only eight days until the election, the Republican presidential candidate tried to rally conservatives by showing his support for the California Civil Rights Initiative (CCRI) which would end race and gender-based preferences in state hiring, contracting and education.

Those who back the initiative need to cast two votes -- one for the ballot measure and one for him, Dole said in a speech, charging that Clinton would do everything possible to preserve, protect and expand quotas.

"The overwhelming majority of Americans and Californians believe as I do that we should promote equal equality for all, without regard to race or gender ... but at the same time we believe it is wrong to use quotas, set-asides and other preferences," Dole said.

"Opponents of CCRI falsely charge that it is merely a response to the anger of white males. But we have seen, in case after case, that quotas and preferences have also hurt women and Asian-Americans," Dole told a specially selected, mostly white audience.
He faced an angry crowd of protesters after his speech.

Dole has previously endorsed the initiative, which is opposed by Clinton, and called for ending similar federal programmes. To replace affirmative action, Dole called for preferences based on income rather than race or gender, vigorously enforcing existing civil rights laws and a new emphasis on education.

In an interview with CNN on Monday, Dole at times appeared resigned to losing the election, saying, "It will either be one way or the other, but I'm not going to jump off a building - jump or go over some cliff.

In the waning days of his campaign, Dole's advisers have decided to step up their focus on affirmative action and immigration, two emotional issues in this key state which has 54 of the needed 270 electoral college votes to win the White House. Polls show a majority of voters back CCRI.

In a sign of how much trouble Dole has in California, where a recent Los Angeles Times poll shows him 20 points behind, he campaigned later on Monday in conservative Orange County with running mate Jack Kemp -- one place he should be far ahead.
Dole said on Sunday he considered affirmative action and immigration wedge issues, a term for sensitive issues used to divide voters.

But Dole, who has supported affirmative action in the past, tried to argue that his support for the California initiative was a move to unite Americans and an extension of his civil rights commitment -- saying politicians should not grandstand on the sensitive issue.
He quoted former President John Kennedy and Minnesota Democratic Sen. Hubert Humphrey, a civil rights champion, in making his case.

"We are talking about the American ideal," Dole said. "The ideal is not a search for special legal privileges, gained at the expense of others ... It is a prinicipled belief in human equality. This is something we cannot compromise without changing the meaning of the United States."

Dole said Clinton had eliminated only one out of more than 160 federal programmes granting preferences and tried to carve out new quotas. "Not only does the Clinton administration oppose CCRI, it has worked to defend and expand racial preferences," Dole said.
Clinton has called for mending, not ending preference programmes, saying government action is still needed to combat discrimination in the United States.
